utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There may have been some confusion as to whether we would start at 10.00, but I do understand, Mr. Krajisnik, that your dentist fell ill. I also was informed that you would now see the dentist on Thursday morning, so we would have a late start on Thursday morning. Then I do understand, Mr. Krajisnik, that you have provided the registrar with a document in B/C/S. May I just have a look at it? This is, it seems, a part of an --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May we have one, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to be a copy of pages 216 up to 218 of a book written by Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's "Cunning Strategy," I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, could you explain what this document -- why you provided this -- I may have asked for it, but I don't remember that. Could you please explain in one word why we receive it now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are two documents, maybe you only have one before you. Actually, I was only trying to assist the Chamber and the Office of the Prosecutor. Yesterday we spoke about whether someone said they were advocating an Islamic state and the moving in of people from Sandzak, and this is evidence to this effect. So I think it's useful for you to have it, and I can tell you exactly where this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Krajisnik, I leave it to the parties -- I leave it to the parties whether they want to present any documentary evidence in support of your testimony. For example, I can imagine that if a certain answer has been given to a certain question, that perhaps in re-examination that Mr. Josse would say: Well, I want to present this because it's -- it is the basis on which you -- but unless the parties would take a different position - I'm looking to both parties - I think that if you have any document, tell us that it exists and we then leave it to the parties, whether they'll ask you to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is a bit hesitant to create a huge collection of whoever wrote about the events in the early 1990s because it may not come as a surprise to you that it mainly adds to the different views on what happened at that time, and the Chamber wants to concentrate mainly on the evidence presented here. This is not, by all means, excluded, but to have this spontaneously, not only brought to our attention that it exists, but spontaneously introduced might be a step too far. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst I, with respect, broadly speaking, agree with what Your Honour said, I wouldn't want Mr. Krajisnik to be in any way dissuaded from bringing to the Chamber documents, particularly original documents, as opposed to book extracts the day after a particular piece of cross-examination which he says demonstrates an assertion put to him is wrong. I would not like him to -- not to do, so it's a double negative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse, I mainly agree with you. Of course I was mainly focussing now on the type of document that is in front of us. As I said before, I think that -- what I said is we are hesitant to create a huge collection of whoever wrote about the events. That, of course, focussed very much on this type of documents. If there is any specific document which would support your answer or would be relevant in the context of an answer you have given on a question, of course you're invited to come with it. Draw the -- first of all, the attention of the parties to the existence of such a document, then the parties will be the first to decide whether or not they want to look at that document and to decide whether they want to introduce it. If the parties would finally say: We're not going to introduce this, not to tender this document in evidence, it's always up to the Chamber to say, we nevertheless would like to have it, and then you might invited to give it to us. So for the time being, I would be inclined to return this and -- but, of course, Mr. Josse and Mr. Tieger, I take it you will --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but you have my response. You gave me a task. You have my response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the next matter then. Yes. What I see that you have, not always in three lines, but you have given a short explanation of what the documents were that you gave in the bundle. My counting to three sometimes is a bit different from yours, but I also see that there are some which are even less than three lines, Mr. Krajisnik. It corresponds to that extent, I would say, to 90 per cent of what I asked you to do, and I take it that this has now been put in priority order of importance? That is, most important document first --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this will be the first document -- yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have highlighted the important documents in yellow, the more important ones. The ones that are not highlighted, as I was going in order, those are the less important documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there are more important than unimportant documents. Mr. Krajisnik, as a matter of fact, I invited you to -- I invited you to indicate the priority order. You still can do so by adding handwritten -- perhaps you take the alphabet, A, B, C, D, et cetera, A being the most important one among the important ones. Because we really -- now you have left to us the choice 1, 2, 3 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can do that here. I can prioritise the ones highlighted in yellow during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because we have now to make up our mind as to the priority among the first 21. So I suggest that we return -- or at least -- do you still have one copy left for yourself, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If you would please indicate clearly, among the yellow ones, which is the most important ones, so just priority order, and at the same time the parties could be provided already with the copies of it. We should keep one for translation -- we asked for it, so I take it that the Chamber has sent it to CLSS and asked it to be translated with priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one comment, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As urged by the Court, we will, of course, consider the suggestions made by the Chamber this morning with respect to this procedure. But one matter does come to mind, and that is that whatever the outcome, we want to ensure that there continues to be a clear distinction between the time -- any time consumed in that process and the time allocated to the OTP for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Mr. Tieger, you may have seen that in the decision we gave on the Defence, we had a kind of an estimate of the average effective time for [indiscernible] witness. We, well, most likely, of course, will apply a similar standard. And we were talking in about in 15 days. What has not been done yet is -- 15 days was for Prosecution and Chamber. We have not made a division there yet. We will consider that soon. And of course there, as well as always with the Defence, we'll take into account also how cross-examination is conducted. Please proceed in order not to lose any further time. Yes, Mr. Josse, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one or two procedural matters; they could wait until the end of the session. However, could I just again mention the very last answer that Mr. Krajisnik gave yesterday and urge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen an e-mail on that. As a matter of fact, to read the answer again to Mr. Krajisnik, I suggested yesterday that we first -- what we first should do is to listen to what Mr. Krajisnik said. Of course, I can't do it myself, but we should not put a translation right or wrong and see. But let's first look at what the actual spoken words in B/C/S were and start on the basis of that rather than on a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I could explain why we didn't do that. That in itself would take me some time. I simply invite the Chamber to proceed in a way that it would had this not been at the end of the session - namely, sought clarification - by asking the witness -- it's the second sentence of that answer that's the problem, as far as the Defence are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the Chamber is firm that we should start with the words spoken. If you say that would have taken me too much time, I'm offering to you in the first break to -- because it's for the Chamber, of course, it's important as well to see whether I can have the assistance of some native B/C/S speakers and to listen to the -- ask them to listen to the tape and ask them to listen carefully what was said in B/C/S and ask for a translation again of those words and to also ask them whether there's any doubt as to whether these original words --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour's more or less identified the problem. If Your Honour does it that way, I have no objection whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If there's any doubt as to what he actually said in B/C/S, then of course the next step would be to invite the witness to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could raise the other matters just before the end of this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. You know when, more or less, to expect the breaks. So -- yes. May I then take it that -- has the tape been listened again by --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It has not. It has not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's the first step we'll do, whether there's any ambiguity in what he said. If there's no ambiguity, we start on the basis of the B/C/S; if there's ambiguity, we'll follow another route.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger. But Mr. Krajisnik, I would first like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If it hasn't been done already, I'd like the anticipated materials for today distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but one of the two procedural matters is precisely this, and it might be better, actually, on reflection, for me to deal with it now. I spoke to Mr. Harmon about this yesterday. I am anxious that Mr. Krajisnik be in a position to take with him back to the UNDU any document that has already been put to him in cross-examination. My learned friends, I think, have no objection to that; however, they do object to him being able to take any document with him back to the UNDU which has not yet been put to him in cross-examination. Now, frankly, I'm not in a position to argue with that. The difficulty is a logistical one, because of course all the documents are together in one or more binders. So we've basically reached a compromise. However, we need to work out how to execute that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll take care that -- I mean, it's your interest how to split up -- what we could, of course, ask is that whatever -- we take one extra binder. Whatever document has been used should be removed from the old binder and put into a new binder. The new binder can be taken by Mr. Krajisnik to the UNDU. Is that a solution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. It never struck me as a particularly difficult logistical issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So let's work on this basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it that the Chamber doesn't have to look at the implementation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one minor clarification, Mr. -- with respect to the 1991/1992 Assembly sessions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- those -- and early 1993, those bindered materials, Mr. Krajisnik has all those, we know, and so I don't think there's any point in re-copying them and having him add to his archives in the DU, with respect to those only is what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing that matters at this moment is whether he has them in front of himself when questions are put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to turn first to the remarks of Mr. Milojevic at the 24th Session. That would be at page 49 of the English, and in the B/C/S you'll find it at 02149912. Last four digits again, 9912. First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Milojevic was also a minister of the RS government. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, this is -- yes, yes. Yes, it was at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And he was a -- had also been a member of the SDS Executive Board. And his ministerial post was, as I understand it, the minister of development and spatial planning. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in another government. The name is similar to the one you have used. He was not a minister on the first government; on the second government he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So after the -- so at the time of this session, therefore, he was the minister of development and spatial planning; this session that took place in January of 1993 after the shake-up of the government in late 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that the old government was replaced by the end of the year, and he was a minister designate. And I don't know whether he participated in the first one as a minister or as a professor, but in the second government he was a minister. I don't know in which role he was saying this, but he eventually did become a minister, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what -- Mr. Milojevic who was or was to become the minister of development and spatial planning said at the 24th Session was the following: "One criterion seems unacceptable to me. Owen followed the pre-war ethnical criterion. This criterion is unacceptable, and we have to achieve that it is necessary negotiations to find the way to say that this pre-war" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just point me to the exact paragraph, please, so I can follow? I'm sorry to give you so much trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Best thing to do, if you look right in the middle of the page, you'll see the numerals 50 to 100. And if you look up several lines --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you look up several lines there, you'll see the beginning of the passage to which I'm referring.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So Minister Milojevic is saying: "The post-war criterion is what counts. If he does not believe it, let him find a way to check it, but Serbs will not return to Tuzla the same way Muslims will not return to Brcko. They will be in favour of the exchange." Then he goes on to talk about the massive relocations that took place, comparing them to the relocations of the previous 50 -- or during a period of 50 years, noting that: "During these five months, for sure nearly a million relocated. This is almost a period of a hundred years while the direction is the same. Many migrations from the multi-ethnic to the ethnically clean regions occurred. This principle was not abandoned. We have to insist, I think, that we finish up the job soon, should it be recognised and should we succeed in having it changed in the way that what has happened. This ethnical change to be seen not as a war change but as something which can be finished in peace, should the peace accept it as an accomplished fact. If we could have that, we would practically have our ethnical state." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, Minister Milojevic is talking there about cementing the effect of the ethnic changes, the changes in population and demographics that occurred during the war, as opposed to restoring the pre-war demographic situation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a professor, and you're right, he is talking from a scientific point of view, not as a member of the SDS. And he often said things of this kind, totally uncontrolled and unexpected for us. He was a university professor. You are right in saying that he did say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's what he meant and when he said that: "Serbs will not return to Tuzla the same way Muslims will not return to Brcko," and urged that: "We finish up the job soon," your explanation is he was talking scientifically, rather than urging and -- a policy that should be pursued by the Bosnian -- by the RS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall be very clear. As for movements of population, he spoke as a scientist. And as for whether the job was finished, the point that you're making concerning an incriminating affair, he would often make proposals of this kind that never met with approval. So this second part of his contribution was not met with approval, was not welcomed by the attendees, although there was some people who thought exactly like he did, but not many.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we'll look at who thought exactly like he did in a moment, but first I'd like to turn to similar remarks by Mr. Milojevic at the very next session located at tab 9. That's found at page 54 of the English and at 02 -- 02149992 of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it. Just give me a line that I should follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you can look almost exactly halfway down the page, and you'll see a reference to Vance-Owen.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. "What is it in the Vance-Owen Project," is that the line?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Milojevic is complaining that: "The Vance-Owen Project does not accept resettlement until a situation is resolved as one of the final solution. It proceeds from the pre-war situation as if nothing had happened in the war and massive settlement actually took place." He goes on for a bit, and then if you'll -- as we move on to page 55 of the English, at the second sentence before the end of that long paragraph, Mr. Milojevic concludes: "The peace plan must provide, and that is not contained in it, must check the extent to which this war settlement contains a civilian message and a civilian solution. We have to ensure that in our future diplomatic struggle and prove and show on civilian principles that the war settlement which has taken place is permanent." And again, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Milojevic is referring to the massive changes of population that took place in the previous months, the creation of new ethnic space, and the need to ensure that it remains permanent. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but your interpretation is wrong. He proposes to adopt the Vance-Owen Plan while saying it is a project that may not work out. And it is true that movements of population happened, regardless of whether they were justified or not. But he is saying that the plan needed to be adopted, and it was the general sentiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can find here --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. That's a deflection of what I was talking about. Whether or not he wants the Vance-Owen Plan adopted under some circumstances, Mr. Milojevic is clearly talking here at the 25th Session and was talking in the 24th Session about the need to ensure that the changes in demographics, that the relocations of population that occurred in the previous months remained permanent. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said the interpretation is different. I can confirm what you said without reading, but look at the following sentence and you will see what I mean. If you just take this out of context, then it looks exactly the way you put it. He was just saying that those movements of population happened, whether they -- it was right or not. But he was advocating the adoption of the plan, although everybody else was against it, and you take this sentence in isolation, whereas if you look at the rest it means something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Milojevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Milojevic was reflecting an attitude and, indeed, a policy that was discussed and pursued by the RS following the massive relocations to which Mr. Milojevic referred. Isn't that right? That is, insofar as possible, ensure that the relocations of population remain permanent.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you that this interpretation is not correct, and I can explain why I'm saying that. It is written here, but what you say is right only if you look at it in isolation. He spoke about relocations from both sides, in both directions. He spoke of it as a reality and said that the Vance-Owen Plan should take them into account. He wasn't talking only about the Serbs; he was saying that mutual movements of population need to be taken into account because people would not come back, that things would remain that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Milojevic was referring to the objective that Serbian ethnical space remain as Serbian as possible and that, to the extent possible, Muslims not be permitted to return, that homogenisation be -- to the extent it existed be maintained and, if possible, increased. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just telling you that it's very dangerous to look at this in isolation without looking at the context. He said the Vance-Owen Plan needed to be adopted. It's different when you talk about implementing policy. It's January 1993. What he said was the reality; that people would not come back. He spoke as a scientist. He mentioned the United Nations and other institutions. That's why he said the Vance-Owen Plan needed to be adopted, contrary to the policy of the Serbian Assembly and the Serbian people. That's the context in which he said it. He didn't say that we should cement the situation in which Muslims had left. That's not what he said. He said it happened and the Vance-Owen Plan should be adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then intervene for one second. Mr. Krajisnik, you're drawing our attention to the context. The next lines read: "When we prove that, if they do not recognise that, recognition of the acceptance as permanent of the relocation, we will probably make new friends in the world and then it will be easier for us, even if we go to war again," which I understand to be: We have to accept the Vance-Owen Plan. The Vance-Owen Plan is not very satisfactory, since it does not contain any of the -- not contain the acceptance of the permanent character of the relocation. So, therefore, that's what we have to work at by diplomatic means. We'll make new friends, and even if we're not satisfied we even could go to war again for this. That's one observation which I'd like you to comment on, because you're asking us to look at it in the context. The second one is there seems to be some misunderstanding between you and Mr. Tieger. If Mr. Tieger says: Isn't Mr. Milojevic advocating the permanence of the situation as far as relocation is concerned, you said you should not look at it one-sided. It's not only that the Muslims should not return to Serb territory, but it's also the other way around. I did not understand Mr. Tieger's question to exclude the other side of that mirror, that where it's advocated, that the Muslims should not return, that Mr. Milojevic does not say at the same time that the Serbs should not return to the place where they come from. At least, Mr. Tieger, I don't know whether I misunderstood you, that it -- the one might even be the corollary of the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your understanding is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So Mr. Tieger doesn't say it's only the Serbs -- it's only the Muslims that should not return, but he draws the attention of this element of the totality of the plan of Mr. Milojevic, which says neither Muslims nor Serbs should return to the place. And I read in the context that if this is not, which is not in the Vance-Owen Plan yet, if it is not achieved later on in further negotiations, that with new allies, even a war would be a possibility. Would you please comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krajisnik's microphone be brought closer to him, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I keep it the way it's set for me. I'm saying that Milojevic said that these things had happened, movements of population on both sides. I'm not saying that he isn't noting this as something in favour of our acceptance of the Vance-Owen Plan, which would not be feasible. I'm just saying that he said it as a scientist, because he mentions here a seminar and the United Nations. He was given a raspberry because nobody wanted the Vance-Owen Plan accepted. He wasn't presenting a policy. The policy was different. He was presenting his opinion as a scientist, although he was a minister, if he was a minister. I'm just saying in which role he said this, and it's important to look at the entirety of his contribution instead of staying -- instead of reducing it to an attempt to cement the situation as it was for the sake of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber will not be assisted by any further interpretation of this text at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you mentioned January 1993 and the context. Did Bosnian Serb leaders, including you, discuss the issue of homogenisation and the need to stimulate migration of Muslims in one direction and Serbs in another in order to improve further on the migrations that actual -- that had already occurred and the homogenisation that had already existed in January 1993 or before or after?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After your discovery of yesterday that I said "Turks," something I was never aware of, I don't rule out that I could have said this, too, on another occasion, but that was not my position. But to answer your question, yes, there were certain people who publicly said those things. But the official position was that everybody had the right to return to their home, and it was accepted in every plan. It was not my policy that people should move out, but if you found this passage somewhere, then I must have said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll talk -- we'll talk about the official position in a bit. But let me ask you quickly about who some of those certain people, who publicly advocated homogenisation, and the maintenance and improvement of the situation caused by the relocations of the previous months. Who were those people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember individual people, but I know that at Assembly sessions President Tudjman was frequently quoted speaking on humane relocation. However, it was not our official policy, because our position, as stated under every plan, was that everybody had the right to return to their homes. If you give me a specific example, I will tell you whether it's correct or not. I cannot even -- I cannot remember anyone really. Maybe it was said by some very highly ranked people. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That could very well be the case. Let's turn to tab 19, please. Tab 19 contains the stenographic notes from a meeting of the council for harmonising view-points on state policy held on 21 January 1993, attended by, among others, you, Mr. Krajisnik; Dr. Karadzic; Dr. Koljevic; General Mladic; Slobodan Milosevic; Mr. Jovanovic, the foreign minister for Serbia; and others. And let's turn first to the remarks of Mr. Jovanovic at page 17 of the English and page 19 of the B/C/S. Mr. Jovanovic says, beginning at that second paragraph: "Territorial link with Serbia and Montenegro, that is Yugoslavia, must be secured in a way that is indisputable and not transitional, but it is more important that the territory we get become, as soon as possible, nationally homogenised, but not by ethnic cleansings, ethnic cleansings are frame-ups, thus by peacetime process of population exchange, that is migration and immigration. It is important that everyone realises that life in that future Bosnia is impossible and that everyone starts moving to his parent province. That is the strategic goal we should pursue and which is to be achieved." And he continues ending with the remarks: "If, on the contrary, freedom of movement would result in freedom of residence and mixing of population to our disadvantage, then the things we have achieved would gradually disappear and we would eventually lose everything. Accordingly, that should be our goal, not to direct the topic of discussion to the fact that large number of Serbs have remained in other nation's provinces, to take territories that are suitable for living and then to stimulate migration of our people to our parent provinces and of their people to their provinces. One should be wise to identify how the above can be achieved, but I think that should be our guiding principle." Now, in discussing those things we have achieved, the objective of ethnic homogenisation and the need to stimulate migration to achieve it, Mr. Jovanovic is raising essentially the same issue that Mr. Milojevic was; that is, saying that while a great deal has been achieved over the past months through the relocations of population, that situation needs to be maintained and even improved. Isn't that right? Isn't that the position he was urging at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: His position was a bit broader. He included Yugoslavia and Serbia as well. I can explain what this is all about, because the context of this meeting is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. So first of all, we agree that that was the position he was taking, but you're explaining that he was referring, in addition, to aspects of what could happen or should happen in Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: His position, as read out here, is what it is, but the context is different from that of Milojevic, and I can explain if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, whether or not the context was different, Mr. Jovanovic is talking about the need to maintain, and even improve, national or ethnic homogenisation by stimulating migrations in the territories held by the Bosnian Serbs, in the territory of RS. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. By homogenisation of Serbs he meant the entire Serb ethnic area, Serbs, not only territories. That's important -- that's why it's important to explain what Mr. Milojevic had explained. Then maybe you would draw the right conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The entire Serb ethnic area, including RS. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please let me explain first. You're extracting things out of context without listening to my explanation. It will certainly be useful to you because the more we go on, the greater the misunderstanding. I have to say yes or no. Yes, all this is correct, but I have to explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, please explain.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a meeting held at the initiative of the late Slobodan Milosevic, where we discussed the Vance-Owen Plan. Mr. Jovanovic is speaking against the Vance-Owen Plan here, whereas four months later he brought a letter in which he was in favour of the Vance-Owen Plan. So he was saying one thing here, but five months later he was saying something else. In this discussion, he says the Vance-Owen Plan is not a good one because it does not make homogenisation possible. Mr. Milojevic says the Vance-Owen Plan is a good one because we've already created the homogenisation of the Serbs in Republika Srpska. This same Jovanovic brought us a letter saying we had to accept the Vance-Owen Plan in Bijeljina, because if we didn't they would impose sanctions on us and they did. Here he himself admits that he is an amateur, layperson, even though he was a minister of the interior and a wonderful man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the reaction of the Bosnian Serb leaders to the remarks of Mr. Jovanovic. At page 19 of the English and page 21 of the B/C/S, Dr. Karadzic points -- I'll wait till you find that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic points out that: "The thing Jovanovic is talking about, I think that has already happened to a great extent. There were 50/50 of us in Zvornik, now Zvornik has the same number of inhabitants, around 50.000, and they're all Serbs. Over 24.000 Serbs from Zenica and Central Bosnia arrived and settled in Zvornik." And then he goes on to talk about: "... Serbia assisting by not receiving refugees, that would be a great solution. And that would be a matter of fact, he notes, which nobody could change." So there Dr. Karadzic is acknowledging Minister Jovanovic's endorsement of homogenisation and pointing out to -- in various places, to a large extent, it's already happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic was against the Vance-Owen Plan here, and he supported Mr. Jovanovic; that's the point. And what you said is correct. The Serbs had left -- had gone to one place, the Muslims to another, from Zvornik. And all this is correct. Karadzic later signed the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Shortly afterward you comment on the remarks of both Minister Jovanovic and Dr. Karadzic. That's at page 20 of the English and page 22 of the B/C/S. And you say at that meeting in January of 1993,

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "I'll start with what Mr. Jovanovic stated, as Radovan spoke in the same way. The problem is not 45 per cent of the territory, maybe it's going to 55. What they have taken from ethnically clean Serbian territories and given to them, that is the countless treasure of the territories we used to have. For example, why do they take a part of Bosnian Krajina and annex it to Cazin Krajina because of the Ljubija mine and the bauxite mine in Bosanska Krupa. Those two mines now belong to Cazin Krajina. Another thing, why did they take Posavina, two oil refineries are there, Bosanski Brod and Modrica, Odzaci commerce facilities, Doboj complex." Now, you say that -- there you're talking about what the proposed plan gives to one side or another. That's the general context of what you're talking about there, as you've mentioned before. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not general, but very important and specific. And this is my opinion. It's true I said this and I still think the same way today. I will explain what I wanted to say here, and that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, before you do I need to ask you a few specific questions about what you said.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You referred to the Ljubija mine, that's a mine in a Prijedor. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, near Prijedor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the bauxite mine in Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those were among the countless treasures taken from the Serbs from the territories, as you put it, "we used to have." Correct? Or at least that would be taken under the plan?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if that's the way you look at it, you're right. But I will explain what you can't see in what I said. You're right, however. Ljubija is in the Croatian part, and the Krupa was Muslim majority. I don't know whether Krupa is in Serb ethnical territory, but I would like to explain what I actually meant here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did you actually mean there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan provided maps. Everybody, including Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Jovanovic, were discussing the size of the territory. What I'm saying, it doesn't matter whether it's 45 per cent or 55 per cent. What matters is the resources. I was speaking as an economist. In Central Bosnia, wherever there was an ethnic space in which there were resources, they gave to the Muslims. So if something, in terms of territory, should belong, it's ethnically Muslim, they gave that to the Muslims, too. And what we got were woods and meadows. So what I'm saying as an economist is that we should not focus on the size of the territory but the quality of the territory we get. But you are right, Krupa is a Muslim majority and Ljubija is a Croat, and that is stated in the Cutileiro Plan, but Modrica is not 100 per cent, neither is Brod where the refinery is. But I was referring to the quality of the territory as opposed to its size. That's why we got 49 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We can see on its face that you're referring to the quality; that is, the things you get in the territories you receive rather than the precise size. You say that there, making specific percentages. But in registering your complaint, part of it is that those things about which you were complaining were not being allocated to the Serbs but to the Muslims, is that they were taken from ethnically clean Serbian territories and given to them. Those ethnically clean Serbian territories are, among others, Prijedor and Bosanska Krupa because you refer to them specifically. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Bosanska Krajina is an ethnic area. There are two small Muslim enclaves there. In the other areas, in Sarajevo, which is richer than half of Bosnia-Herzegovina where the Serbs invested, and there are Serbs there, that, too, was given to the Muslims. You have to look at the overall economic context. Krajina, as such, is Serb majority area. I wasn't referring to these two small enclaves, but all of Krajina. Una, the river Una was the border, so it should have belonged to the Serbs. You cannot avoid the fact that Krupa was a Muslim majority municipality. It wasn't a territory that was Muslim majority, but the population. I don't know whether the mine is on the right- or left-hand bank of the river Una. It might be on Serb territory or Muslim territory, I don't know, and Ljubija is actually Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before the conflict began in April of 1991, there were approximately 50.000 Muslims in Prijedor alone. That wasn't an ethnically clean area, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not about Prijedor, it's about the territory. The territory of Prijedor is much more Serb than Muslim. There were more Muslims in the town itself, whereas Ljubija is a separate little town where the Croats are in the majority, not the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the remarks of Mr. Koljevic found at page 22 of the English and page 25 through 26 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Koljevic merges the two discussions, noting that, as he begins: "I think that along with dissimilarities one common thing emerges from Momo's speech and from Mr. Jovanovic's speech earlier on. When maps are in question it's better to insist on the economic principle than on the national." And then he continues: "In short, I think that this, using an economic principle in order to cover up the other one, is very good and it should be combined with something else, if possible." And then he explains how to do that and finally continues at pages 23 -- pages 22 through 23, after he mentions that he travels a great deal around Republika Srpska: "I don't need to tell you what that means. We have" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just tell me where this is, please. Excuse me, is it on page 26?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... "I don't need to tell you what that means. We will have to develop a great political activity" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- "in order to win the people for this and to develop the activity of homogeneous settlement while there is still time." Now, there Mr. Koljevic is doing two things. Number one, he's acknowledging that using an economic argument rather than an ethnic argument is likely to be more persuasive to international negotiators; and two, he's confirming and endorsing the objective of homogenous settlement while there's still time to do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think the paragraph immediately above needs to be read to put it into context. That's my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, are you going to follow that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That can be put in -- I don't think it changes the focus of my -- of the question, and if Mr. Krajisnik wants to read it, he can. I see no point in reading it aloud. It's there for him, but that doesn't change the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm happy with that, as long as Mr. Krajisnik can read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. President, the Prosecutor has confused me more than you have. I can't find it here. I wish to comment on it and I wish to speak correctly. I cannot find the context. I know exactly what happened at that meeting, but the question is a specific one. So could I be pointed to the right place, please, so I can be as specific as possible. I found what you were reading out, yes, but when you skipped over some things, then I got lost. If it's the last passage, yes, then I've found it. Please let me read it. Just a moment, please. I abide by everything Mr. Koljevic said, but I can clarify if there is anything unclear here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I have no additional questions about that and don't require any clarification, unless the Court does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in fact the Bosnian Serb leadership would continue to insist on the effect of the factual situation that had been created during the war and to insist, to the extent possible, that it be maintained. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. That's why I was trying to explain just a while ago. What is correct is that we continued to insist on returning to the original positions of the Cutileiro Plan, where homogenisation of Serb ethnic areas was there precisely in a single unit, not cleansing, not what happened during the war. There were such statements, but that was not the policy. The Vance-Owen Plan abolished the Republika Srpska, and that was the main reason why we opposed it. That's why Mr. Koljevic opposed provinces, and he explained all this. But one needs to understand it. Perhaps I understand this better because I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the insistence was, and I don't want to be -- make sure that we're talking about the same thing, that the demographic situation that had been created during the war be maintained, that now that Zvornik, for example, was a Serbian municipality, as Mr. -- as Dr. Karadzic explained to Minister Jovanovic at the coordination council, it should stay that way, to the extent the Bosnian Serb leadership could control that. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Jovanovic said what the actual situation was that had been created in the war. They said that's the war. After that, they proposed negotiations, and this is contrary to what you've just said, in which there were no wartime gains. And in fact this happened. There are no Serbs in Zvornik or Zenica now. They were not enthusiastic about what had happened. They keep asking for negotiations. They weren't happy that there were no Muslims left in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn next to the 26th Session and some remarks by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That may have to be distributed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, a portion of Dr. Karadzic's remarks to which I'm directing your attention is found at 02150079 in almost the precise middle of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, it's at the second page of English portion provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's just after the reference to Lebanon, Cyprus --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... about India, et cetera. "Had the Muslim leadership," said Dr. Karadzic, "had their composure, they would have got what they got without a drop of blood. Had it been before the war we would have sacrificed more territories than we are prepared to sacrifice now. If we had reached an agreement without a war, we'd made some kind of demarcation between us. Now this is what we have, and the international community will have to recognise the new factual situation. This war has created a new factual situation. Nobody is going to return 50.000 Serbs to Zenica from Zvornik or to Central Bosnia. No way. Cutileiro's map gave us more than half of Zvornik." Now, there, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Karadzic is not talking about just about territory, he's talking about people, isn't he? And he's saying that the Serbs aren't leaving Zvornik, and he's also indicating to the Assembly that the Muslims aren't coming back. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take it out of context, then you're right. He did say this, but he also said something before that, that you have not read out. He's referring to the Vance-Owen Plan here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how does that change the fact that Dr. Karadzic is talking about people and where they're going to be and whether they're going to come back and where they're going to go, whether it's in the context of Vance-Owen or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we have some difficulties in finding --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mine is incomplete as well, Your Honour. I don't have the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got one of two pages, and I've got only one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And since you did not indicate on which page to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My learned friend said it was the second page, in fact, which we don't have. Perhaps it can be put on the ELMO, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could that be put on the ELMO? And could we give a second, again -- yes, to read it. Yes. Please zoom in a tiny little bit. That's fine. Yes. Perhaps, Mr. Tieger, if you will repeat your last question, then we could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I understand that many of these discussions take place while international negotiations are ongoing. My question was: How does that change the fact that Dr. Karadzic is talking about people and where they're going to go and where they're not going to go?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic was explaining the Cutileiro Plan. He made an introduction -- no, excuse me, not the Cutileiro Plan, the Vance-Owen Plan. And he had before him people who are asking him what will happen to us now? Zvornik belongs to the Muslims and we have fled from Zenica. It was for this reason Mr. Karadzic was saying: Nobody's going to drive you out. He says: We need to go on working, and so on. It's a question of politics. If you're saying to people that they have to leave the area to which they have moved, because according to the plan this area is going to be Muslim, at the time the Vance-Owen Plan was being discussed. In May it was signed in Athens. He's saying this for the sake of the deputies, who are saying: What's going to happen to us, because we belong to this province?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the politics was insofar as possible to rely on the factual situation that had been created during the war in addition to the previous ethnical territory and historical arguments that had been made to ensure that Serbs could stay in the territories that RS now controlled and that Muslims couldn't come back. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To show that this is not so, I will show you a map showing that the Serbs agreed to withdraw from 23 per cent of the territory, and this is in Lord Owen's book. I will show you the map where we agreed to this. He was saying this for the sake of politics. He said: We can't accept the plan or they will flee from here. I will bring you the map to show you what our policy was. This was for political purposes. The people would leave the area because it belonged to somebody else's province and they had to flee from Zenica. This was not our policy. The plans show what our policy was, and this was purely for political purposes. I know exactly what they were saying. I'm not saying that some soldiers did not want that; this is a military way of speaking. But I'm telling you that our policy was to go back to negotiations and we were willing to withdraw. There is a map showing from what territories we were willing to withdraw, and this was an enormous concession, in view of the territories we held. I ask that the map be brought tomorrow so I can show this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we would be happy to see the map at an appropriate time, and when we return from the break I want to show you some additional comments relating to the effort to cement the factual situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but before we have a break, Mr. Josse, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I would like to go and see Mr. Krajisnik for two reasons, both of which I have mentioned to my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We've had that discussion and we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I take it it's all within what the Chamber would expect parties to agree upon and that you're allowed, even without further information, to see Mr. Krajisnik on these matters. We'll adjourned until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, CLSS is working on the matter you raised at the beginning of this hearing. We hope to, perhaps already during the next break, to have an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would be very grateful. Your Honour, Mr. Krajisnik was working on the task Your Honour had set him. He's going to complete it at the next break and have it ready thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A couple more questions about the maintenance of the factual situation, as I indicated before the recess. If we could turn first to tab 40 -- excuse me, to the 42nd Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And where to find that now? Is that in --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's being distributed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the parts to which I want to direct your attention are found on pages 02152880 and 02152881?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, found at the first and the second pages of the handout in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, again talking in the context of international negotiations,

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC ACKNOWLEDGES
utterances.text: "We know for a fact we have to relinquish something, that's beyond doubt. In case we want to achieve our first strategic goal, which is to get rid of the enemy in our house" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, that's found at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- we have no cover page, so we cannot place it in time. That would be the -- 42nd Session was when?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 42nd Session, and I thought I had the precise date written down, and I do not. I can have that for the Court in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Whoever knows that first is invited to tell the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could have just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This would be far in 1993 or even later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The -- again, the portion to which I wish to direct your attention, Mr. Krajisnik, and the Court's attention, begins in the English about halfway down right after the numbers about the municipalities that appear. "We know for a fact that we have to relinquish something; that's beyond doubt. In case we want to achieve our first strategic goal, which is to get rid of the enemy in our house," meaning the Croats and Muslims, "and not to be together in one state anymore. All divorces are costly, and we have to relinquish some things, but we are winners and we not only control a large territory, but we own it." And then Dr. Karadzic continues after references to those towns and places of worship and traditional hills that are important to the Bosnian Serbs. He says: "What he think and what I think is that the factual situation can be recognised. A war ended with a draw like this only very rarely and such territory was returned only very rarely. Montenegro did not return Skadar, but it returned 30 per cent of the territory under its control." And he continues talking about things to return and concludes: "We have to dance along the edge of the abyss. We know that we must relinquish something. We know we have to cut a finger off and we know it will be painful, but we cannot allow ourselves to have both hands cut off let alone have our throat cut. Even without hands a man is still a man, but he cannot take care of himself, nor can he feed himself or defend himself. Our desire is to move further from the factual situation, and this means a defeat of one side. This means that we have to move towards the factual situation and to give something up in the factual situation so we can be the ones to decide what it is that we'll relinquish and not have them take whatever they want." Now, first, Mr. Krajisnik, in the reference to both moving further from the factual situation and then moving toward the situation -- towards the factual situation, Dr. Karadzic is referring to efforts after the massive displacement and relocations of people in 1992, efforts to further concentrate Muslims or pack Muslims into small areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not right, Mr. Prosecutor, and I can explain. The meaning of the words of Mr. Karadzic is clearly stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, the factual situation he's talking about is the factual situation on the ground. Correct? That is, the situation that exists with respect to where -- which territories are controlled and to where the members of the ethnic groups now reside. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. The factual state is what the armies of the three parties were holding under their control; that's the war and that much is true. That's the factual situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Dr. Karadzic is acknowledging that Bosnian Serbs may be obliged to relinquish some portion of what they hold, but they want to relinquish as little as possible. That's the reference to the finger versus the hand or the throat. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't mean that. He meant that we can't make our map in advance. We don't have our own proposal. That's what's written here. Why would we cut off one finger before knowing the outcome of the negotiations? That's the meaning of his words, because it's very dangerous to draw a map - that's what Karadzic was saying - in which you have a large territory reduced to 49 per cent, because the people from that territory will pack their bags, and you don't know yet whether the negotiations will ultimately grant you that territory. So the issue is how to reduce 65 per cent to 49 per cent, and you can see that he's ready to relinquish part of the territory, but he doesn't know which part of the territory. That's the meaning of Mr. Karadzic's words here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the -- Dr. Karadzic was aware of the situation on the ground, aware that the Bosnian Serbs had created realities that didn't exist before the conflict, and was claiming territories based on what he saw as the right that comes out of that new reality. Wasn't that a position he maintained to -- he and the other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, including you, maintained during the course of the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way you put it, although it was being said. It was a matter of tactics in negotiations, but there was readiness to create a map as the factual situation on the ground was. And that's what we did. But when negotiations are ongoing, then you put forward various tactical elements and you even use tactics with relation to your own MPs to get them to support your position. There was a plan, and it was only a matter of tactics how to achieve that plan, which was not always palatable, even to the MPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the exact words of Dr. Karadzic in that respect. And if we could turn to the 46th Session, please, at tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the previous session was -- and that is the 42nd Session was held on 18 and 19 July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have the 42nd Session --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The 46th was held on November 9th through 11th and the 23rd of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we have the -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the portion of that session to which I want to draw your attention begins at 02153381 in the B/C/S and continues on to 02153382. And there Dr. Karadzic states -- oh, I'm sorry. And it's page 157, not obviously of the tabbed portioned, but labelled below 157, which is about the fourth page in the extract in English.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it on the page you just told me the number of, 3381?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It starts at the bottom of the page and it begins: "Our goal is to create a state. How big it will be, we do not know, but it has to be in one piece, and in order" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just give me a moment to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. That's the fourth sentence from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "... and in order for the state to exist, it has to be in one piece. We have to maintain this reality as long as the world accepts this idea. We have created new realities. Speaking in narrow terms, Zvornik used to be 60/40 to the advantage of Muslims, but the Serbs from Zenica came, they occupied Kozluk. The Muslims left for Europe and I don't know where else. And then those gentlemen told us: Who gives you a right to ask for Zvornik? We said that the whole Bosnia was Serbian land, that's the history, but it is not what we are interested in. Who gives you a right to request Zvornik now? We requested Zvornik based on the right which comes out of a new reality. This war had created the new reality. It has never happened in history that the war did not create a new reality. This war has created the new reality. There are now the Serbs from Zenica here. If you want to give Zvornik to the Muslims, then you have to wage a new war in order to expel these Serbs back to Zenica. We request Zvornik according to this right." Mr. Krajisnik, this is an explicit acknowledgment, isn't it, by Dr. Karadzic of the insistence that the consequences of the military campaign in 1992, in 1993 created a new reality that the Bosnian Serb leadership was going to insist be maintained insofar as possible.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, I'm telling you that that's not the way it is and I want to explain. To some extent I've already explained it. This is just rhetoric. I know this conversation that took place with Mr. Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg about Zvornik on the terrace overlooking the Zvornik lake, but he needed to pacify the people because Zvornik was supposed to belong -- to be given to another ethnic community, in which case the Serbs would have packed their bags. So he was trying to appease the people, because everybody would withdraw, including the army. And just at that time there were maps, current maps, on which we had withdrawn from large territories. So he's saying: I don't know what we're going to give back, but we'll have to give back something. But at the same time he had to appease the people and the army, because the army would also leave the territories that they thought would ultimately not be ours. It's not that we were pushing for maintaining the factual situation; we were pushing for negotiations. We didn't know what we were going to do. We had a large territory and we had to give back something. We gave back Serb territories and got, in return, ultimately some Muslim territories. In every discussion, the factual situation was advocated to prevent the army from withdrawing from that area, because people were telling us: Tell us what's going to be ours so we know where to go, and we didn't know what to answer. It would have been a catastrophe if Karadzic said: The things we are holding now are not ultimately going to be ours, people would have withdrawn, the army would have pulled out. No politician would have done that. I know exactly what I'm talking about as far as Zvornik is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And to the extent that the Bosnian Serbs were obliged to relinquish any territory to the Muslims, then there would be efforts made to prevent Muslims from moving out of the territories they had into Serb territory. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Let me give you an example. We lost Glamoc, Grahovo, Drvar, all of them Serb ethnic areas in the western region on the map. However, factually speaking, Muslims had captured it. We lost the Serb Sarajevo that we used to hold. Factual situation was different from the map. And the factual situation represented nothing, counted for nothing in negotiations, and it wasn't our policy. These things and things of that kind were said in order to keep the army in place. Even I had to say things like that, otherwise the army would have pulled out. And even so, some people deserted from the front line. Policy is one thing, and the rhetoric required to implement a policy is something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask you -- let me try to understand you, Mr. Krajisnik. Do you say, for example, language which is used here: "This war has created new a reality. They are now the Serbs from Zenica here. If you want to give Zvornik to the Muslims, then you have to wage a new war in order to expel the Serbs back to Zenica." Is this what you call rhetoric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I remember exactly that sentence. When Mr. Karadzic told Mr. Owen in Zvornik: Serbs had been expelled into Zvornik and Muslims left Zvornik, he said: I don't see any way of returning both ethnic communities, and they are both refugees, and he sounded here as a warmongerer, just to get the point across to our people that they should stay on in Zvornik until we know exactly whether we would have to return it or not. That kind of language was inappropriate, maybe, in -- by our standards of today, but at that time it had to be put that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So Dr. Karadzic told the Bosnian Serb Assembly on repeated occasions that the factual situation and the new reality had to be maintained, and he told the same thing to Mr. Owen, in a slightly more diplomatic way?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At every meeting Mr. Karadzic said and repeated that the lines and the factual situation had to be preserved. At every meeting he said: Lines and factual situation have to be preserved. And at every meeting he had to face questions like: What are our territories? What is our plan so we know to defend only these things and let go of the other things? He said -- he answered: I don't know what the plan is. We'll find out through negotiations. Negotiations will eventually result in a map. And Milan Trbojevic, a witness here, said that on hundreds of occasions he asked Karadzic: What is the plan? What are we supposed to defend? And Karadzic never knew what to say. You have a large territory and you are faced with the problem of deciding what territories to give back. And in order not to erode the lines, you have to use this kind of language when talking to the people so that they stay on. And of course he had to pepper his speech with historical references in order to support his argument. It was not a question of factual situation. Nobody managed to maintain the factual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I asked you earlier what would be the case if the Bosnian Serbs were obliged to relinquish some territory and whether or not Muslims would be discouraged, prevented, delimited from moving into Serb territory, and you told me that was not the case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't quite understand. If Serbs were to relinquish certain territories, would we be against the Muslims settling or resettling there? Is that what you are asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. Not in the territories that were allocated to the Muslims, but in moving from the territories allocated to the Muslims to Serbian territory, to RS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In every agreement we accepted and signed that everybody had the right to return to their original home. It's possible that somebody stated otherwise somewhere here, but such a clause exists in every agreement, accepted by all the three parties. And it was of our own free -- sorry. It was up to people to decide. It was their choice whether they wanted to return or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you and Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic and Minister Jovanovic talked about strategies for maintaining and even improving homogenisation. And in respect to your remark just now that it's possible that somebody might have stated otherwise, well, why don't we look to Dr. Karadzic at the 39th Session of the National Assembly on the 24th and 25th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's found at tab 16, Your Honours, at page 88 of the English, and page 71 or 02152322 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krajisnik, that's found in approximately the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where Dr. Karadzic says, again talking about negotiations: "It can happen that either they will try to dump all the Muslims on us or they will try to divide Bosnia at Sandzak, one half to Serbs, one half to Croats. In that case they will try to dump Tuzla on us. We may be in a position to have to accept that, but we will delimit them in some kind of autonomous province theirs, from which they will not be able to move freely and settle in our areas." Now, there Dr. Karadzic is assuring the Bosnian Serb deputies, the Bosnian Serb people that to the extent possible all efforts will be made to ensure that Muslims don't settle into the areas that have been claimed by and taken by the Bosnian Serbs. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. I really cannot make a connection here and answer this. It says something completely different here, so I cannot confirm this. Can you put your question a little more clearly, please. He is not laying claim to Muslim areas here; he is speaking about the possibilities, in his view, of solving the Bosnian crisis. And this actually happened later on. The Muslim-Croatian federation has been established and the rest is Republika Srpska, so Bosnia has been divided. And he's talking about what he learned, he's talking about the plans. And he's putting forward here the different versions of what the outcome might be. Could you please put your question again a little more clearly?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I had asked you about the Bosnian Serb position with respect to free movement of Muslims back into the areas that were now controlled by and -- by the Bosnian Serbs. And we were talking about whether or not Muslims were going to be permitted to come back to the areas held by Bosnian Serbs. That was clearly the subject we were talking about before, and so I directed your attention to remarks by Dr. Karadzic where he said: "We will delimit them in some kind of autonomous province of theirs, from which they will not be able to move freely and settle in our areas."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one segment. In the very same plan, Mr. Karadzic signed that everyone can go back to their homes, and that was the policy, not this. If you read everything he says, he says: I don't know what will happen. And he presents the different versions. And he says: What are we going to do with Tuzla? Tuzla isn't ours; it's something invented. And he's talking about something that will not happen that actually didn't happen, that Tuzla will be given autonomy. But please, find the plan and you will see that all three sides signed firmly that everyone can go back to their own homes. This is not the plan. These are his fantasies about what might happen and what Europe and America might think about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I intervene for one moment. It happens again and again and again, Mr. Krajisnik, that Mr. Tieger is putting to you some text, and then you explain that it finally was not done the way as said at this moment. Let's clearly distinguish between what was said at that moment. So, for example, in this case you would say this is what you say is right, that's what Mr. Karadzic said at the time. It was not our policy, and you can learn that from the final agreement that was concluded at a later stage he signed, where you'll not find this in this anymore. Let's clearly distinguish. And it struck me several times that Mr. Tieger is putting a question to you and that you are responding in a way which is not directly related to the question. There's nothing wrong with saying: It's true, that's what Dr. Karadzic said, it suggests that Muslims should not be returned to Tuzla, but finally in the negotiations a different position was taken and you can see that from the result of the negotiations. Then it's perfectly clear what was said at the time and what then, after that, happened. And it happened a couple of times that you more or less say: You are interpreting this wrong, not because on the basis of what was said at that time, but on the basis of the events that happened later. Let's clearly distinguish the two. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I understood the question at the end: Was what Mr. Karadzic said here your policy? I don't remember Karadzic saying this. I can read it, and of course when I read this I can say: Yes, that's what it says here. But with respect to the policy, I'm explaining what the policy was. This was rhetoric, and that's my response to all the questions. What I am arguing here is that there was no actual plan here; it was only an imaginary plan. I am answering the questions as I understand them, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think whether Mr. Karadzic at that moment expressed policy or just his own views is not part of the question, at least I didn't understand it, and I just re-read the questions. But, Mr. Tieger, you may have heard that Mr. Krajisnik understood the question in a different way as I take it from what I understood you wanted to put it. Let's try to keep this as clear as possible under all circumstances. So if there's any difference between what was said and what was the policy, let's also distinguish between the two and say: Do you understand this, Mr. Karadzic -- is the meaning of what Mr. Karadzic said so and so and so, and then it's a different question on whether that was generally accepted SDS policy, might be his own policy, it might be -- but let's avoid that question and answers are mainly based on misunderstanding each other. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, Mr. Krajisnik, there's a difference, we agree, between what one hopes to achieve and wants to achieve and what one is able to achieve. Correct? That's a simple matter of general understanding.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're completely right. Very many people had certain wishes, whereas the reality was different, and also people in official positions who wanted one thing while the reality was another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
