utterances.text: Number 2, it is correct, isn't it, that Dr. Karadzic is saying here that at least the desire - and he says "we" throughout, so I take it he's meaning the desire of the Bosnian Serbs - is to deter or discourage the free movement of Muslims from whatever territory they're allocated into whatever territory Serbs retain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, this is two questions in one, which creates, again, a similar situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first ask whether what Mr. Karadzic is saying here is an expression of a desire; and then the next question is whether it was just Dr. Karadzic, his desire, or whether the use of the word "we" would reflect that he was not talking in the pluralis majestatis but whether he was talking as a representative of the Bosnian Serbs. This is exactly an example of what I meant. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, Mr. Krajisnik, it is correct, isn't it, that Dr. Karadzic is expressing there the desire to deter or discourage the free movement of Muslims from whatever territory they are allocated into Bosnian Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably what is written here, but I guarantee that that was not his wish when he said that because he was pursuing a realistic policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when he said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you're -- Mr. Krajisnik, now you're doing the same. You're mixing up what was in the mind of Dr. Karadzic and what his words say. So the first step is if I say: The sun is shining, that has the actual meaning of no clouds being before the sun. Yes, that's -- so the first thing is how we should understand it from the language itself, and of course the next step is whether what was said, whether these words in this particular situation would have had a different meaning for the person who uttered this. So we have to clearly define this. Just to give an example, if we say: The sun is shining, it means there are no clouds before the sun, there are no clouds covering that territory. And if you would then say: But in the specific circumstances it should be understood differently because the words were uttered by a pilot, who was above the clouds, then it becomes clear that the normal meaning of these words would not apply in the specific circumstances. So here, if someone says -- whether these words should be understood in its normal meaning, that free movement should be discouraged, whether that's the normal meaning of the words. And then of course the second question is whether you have any specific knowledge why Mr. Karadzic, using these words, would nevertheless have had something different in his mind. We should clearly make a distinction to that, what was said, what is the normal meaning of these words, and could we apply the normal meaning of these words under those circumstances. That's -- I would like to have matters as clear as possible and do it step by step and not confuse everything, as happened this morning, both in your answers and in the questions. I would rather now invite Mr. Tieger to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't remember these words. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- we are working on the basis of this tape-recording. You don't have to remember -- the first question is: What is the normal meaning of these words? Mr. Tieger is seeking confirmation of whether there's any misunderstanding about these words. If you say: It goes without saying, then I would say -- then just say, yes, that's what he said. And then you add whatever you know -- whatever you know, which would cause us to -- not to accept that the one who uttered those words was meaning something which is the normal understanding of these words, but whether he had something different in his mind. Let's proceed. And Mr. Tieger is asking on the basis of the text he reads to you, which is the text of the tape-recording, the transcribed tape-recording of the 39th Session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't doubt this. I'm not casting doubt on this text --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, that's not the issue, but you said: I don't remember these words. We're working on the basis of what we see here. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it correct that Dr. Karadzic was communicating to the deputies of the Bosnian Serb Assembly at that time that it was the position of the Bosnian Serb leadership that, to the extent possible, Muslims would be prevented or deterred from moving from whatever territories they were allocated under an agreement into Bosnian Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. That's what I want to explain. That's not what Karadzic said when he uttered these words, although that's what is written down here. He was saying: Were something to happen that never happened, that's what he was saying. He wasn't saying: If this happens, because he was not referring to a concrete plan. He was only trying to calm their fears so that they wouldn't leave this territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, whatever motivation you attribute to his comments, it is correct, isn't it, that he wanted the deputies to understand -- he was communicating to the deputies that this was the position of the Bosnian Serb leadership. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was communicating to them as if the position of the Serb leadership had another goal. It was as if this was the position of the leadership and as if this was his position, while it really wasn't his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A few moments ago we looked at Dr. Karadzic saying that it would be necessary to wage a new war if one wanted to give Zvornik to the Muslims. Was that the position you took as well, Mr. Krajisnik, that a new war would be necessary to undo the reality and -- that had separated the Serbs from the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to Zvornik, this was tactical in order to calm down the people who had moved there. Yes, he said that, but it was not his standpoint or mine or anyone's. He was just saying that to persuade the people to stay there. I agree he said that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I think the question was whether that was your position as well. That was the question. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two questions. Yes, I will tell you whether it was my position. It was not my position. And if ever I said this, if I did, I would have said it for political purposes, but it was never ever my position that someone could not return to their home. It was always my position that everyone should be able to return to their homes, and that was what I always advocated at negotiations. If ever I said that anywhere, and I don't think I did, it was only for political purposes to calm people down and to assuage their fears.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at where you said it and what you said. If we could turn next to --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- tab 5. Tab 5 is a transcript of a TV broadcast of the meeting of Serbian unity in Banja Luka. We -- the Court has had an opportunity to see a portion of that on screen. That was held on 21 August 1994. Your comments, Mr. Krajisnik - if I can just have a moment - will be reflected at page -- approximately beginning around page 7 of the B/C/S. And in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's page 9, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you begin by saying: "Dear brothers and sisters, my dear people of the Krajina on both sides of the union, having heard these wonderful words by my predecessors, I feel great satisfaction at being at this gathering here today." And just so you know, the wonderful words which are being referred to earlier, those include the remarks of Mr. Kupresanin at pages 4 through 5 of the English, who says, among other things: "There can be no Muslim state on land that has been forever Serbian. There is no Muslim people, and the entire world knows this. There are only Serbian people in these parts." And the words of Mr. Brdjanin at page 5 of the B/C/S and page 6 of the English, who says, among other things: "Those leftist forces who are offering us co-existence again must know it is the obligation of Serbs over the next hundred years to wipe their feet from the foul non-Christians who have befouled this soil of ours." And your remarks continue, Mr. Krajisnik, until the point where you say: "We simply want to separate because we cannot live together. I must add something to the discussion and to the address delivered by Mr. Kupresanin. If the Muslims do not wish to be Serbs, if they don't recognise it, I believe them because I can only feel" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just tell me where this is. You're skipping over and I can't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You started from the beginning, and now I can't find this concerning Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That can be found at page 9 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, while Kupresanin is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I can't find Kupresanin, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Kupresanin is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the bottom of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Kupresanin is -- is page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I found Kupresanin, but I can't find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 8 and following, it starts -- you start on page 7, Mr. Krajisnik, and then it continues on page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's page 12 of the English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And page 9 of the B/C/S. And now I'll -- is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll continue: "If the Muslims do not wish to be Serbs, if they do not -- if they don't recognise it, I believe them because I can only feel sorry for anyone who does not know and who does not want to be a Serb because he does not know how beautiful and glorious it is. That's why we need to separate. It would take a great war to force us to live together again. We don't need war to separate us; we are already separate. The war would be necessary for someone to assemble us together in the same state. Our goal is that we are fighting for today becomes a united state. May God grant us this. All the territory now called Republika Srpska or Serbian Krajina will be Serbia." Now, that's an example of the same position taken by Dr. Karadzic at the 46th Session; that is, to undo the reality that had been created, to undo the massive relocations and redistribution of people it would take another war because, to the extent possible, you and Dr. Karadzic were not going to permit that to be undone.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is so wrong, Mr. Prosecutor. I cannot understand how you can interpret it like this. You have to read the whole text, and then you'll see what I said, and my response to Mr. Kupresanin. That is not correct, for someone to return us to a unitary Bosnia, that's what I meant to say, not to assemble us together. We have accepted Bosnia here. Let me comment on each thing that you said, about Kupresanin, about the Muslims, about everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I mentioned two things, and then we'll move on from there. I mentioned Brdjanin saying: We have to wipe our feet from the foul non-Christians, and Kupresanin -- so let me ask you about -- what was it you wanted to comment about Brdjanin's comment? And first of all, let me clarify, the non-Christians means the Muslims. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it refers to the Muslims, but I did not comment on Mr. Brdjanin. That was a completely wrong discussion. I was commenting only on Kupresanin's statement. And rhetorically I said these wonderful statements simply in order to gloss over a statement I did not agree with. I will comment on Kupresanin's statement. Mr. Kupresanin denied the existence of the Muslims. He said they were former Serbs, and everybody applauded. They applauded all kinds of nonsense. And ineptly I said if the Muslims didn't want to be Serbs we had to believe them. What I meant to say by this was that they had the right to be Muslims; that's what I still think today. And then I wanted to tell all these people who were listening that it's nice to be a Serb and that it's sad that they don't want to be Serbs. But you can't tell someone that he has to be a Serb if he wants to be a Muslim; you can see that from here. But I had to put it this way because there were so many people there and I couldn't say: Kupresanin, you're a criminal. What politician would say that? I just said nicely: Well, we should believe them when they say they're Muslims. You have no right to force someone to be a Serb if he's not. That's what I meant to say by these words. I wasn't denying the Muslims their right to be a nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention quickly to two matters, first of all, to the -- to at least one of the proposed tactics employed by the Bosnian Serbs in efforts to prevent the return of Muslims to places where they resided before, and I need to, in that respect, direct your attention to two sessions. The first is the 37th Session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that needs to be distributed. And I'm going to direct Mr. Krajisnik's attention to two remarks there. The first is by Mr. Maksimovic beginning at page 126 of the English and page 93 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Maksimovic's remarks begin in almost exactly the middle of the page at what is the third full paragraph on that page, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAKSIMOVIC SAYS
utterances.text: "What I'd really like to see here is a firm attitude that the Muslims and the Croats will not be allowed to return to the areas under our rule. Accordingly, we should not return to the areas that will be under the Croatian rule. I think we should be decisive about this, otherwise I'm afraid that those people from Sandzak will occupy Srbinje," that was once Foca, "and surrounding areas because there are too many of them in that area. So we should take a firm position and ban any of their returns to the territories we have gained through these international combinations, just so that we prevent that the international community cheat on us after we sign this. I must say this is very difficult for you, and I understand that, however, our people believe when we are making the compromises, we are more concerned about their destiny than the destiny of our own people. I do not care if the Muslims who live at all where they will live, whether they will have a country or not, I'm not interested in that. The only thing I am interested in is my people and the territory where my people live. Therefore, any thought about having 500 or more Muslims within our future country is out of the question." And then if I could turn your attention -- the Court's attention to page 132 of the English and page 97 of the B/C/S. These are remarks by Dr. Karadzic, and it's the second paragraph of his remarks shown on that page, Mr. Krajisnik. "As to the return of the refugees, I owe an answer to Vojo's question. According to the international law, we have no right to ban the return of the refugees. In principle, all refugees can return, but I would suggest -- I would just add one sentence. This also has to be a two-way process. The Muslims and the Croats accepted a two-way process. Later on Owen asked me: Why do you insist on the two-way process? But when the Serbs from Zvornik return [realtime transcript read in error "returned"] to Zenica, then the Muslims from Prijedor will return to Prijedor; therefore, it must be a two-way process. In accordance with international law, we cannot declare a ban of the return on refugees." Now, in responding to Mr. Maksimovic's comments in that manner, wasn't Dr. Karadzic explaining a strategy, indeed a cunning strategy, to forestall and prevent the return of Muslims to territories held by the Serbs, notwithstanding the spirit of the international agreements?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this started a polemic. Mr. Karadzic said according to international conventions, the return of refugees has to be allowed. And when responding to warmongering statements, he said things that would be pleasing to their ears. He was far from having the meaning that you suggest; he was trying to counter those warmongering statements. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, let's distinguish motivation from meaning. Is it correct that Dr. Karadzic was communicating to Mr. Maksimovic and the other representatives of the Serbian people assembled there, that he had devised a stratagem to prevent Muslims from returning to Serb areas? Isn't that what he was communicating?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Instead he devised a stratagem for them to accept the plan because he had already signed it. He had signed that they would be returning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One more time and then I will abandon that. Isn't it correct that what Dr. Karadzic was saying there, what he was communicating in the passage I just read to you, is that by the inclusion of this two-way process provision there was a way to satisfy Dr. -- the concerns of Dr. Maksimovic and others about the risk of Muslims returning to Serb territory? And I don't want to hear again about why he said it; I just want you to confirm whether or not the plain meaning of those words communicated to the deputies was that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that he said this to Mr. Maksimovic, but he also said there were international conventions. He said those two things to the gathering; whereas Mr. Maksimovic is an intelligent man and he knows that international conventions have priority, are superior to, the clause that Mr. Karadzic may have included. It's true he said what you just quoted, but he also said there were international roles that have primacy over whatever Mr. Karadzic included or didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there are ways --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you allow me to, if it would help to -- if I were to tell you what I, as a non-native speaking person understand this to be, and let's also check on the basis of the original whether the ambiguity I found does exist, yes or no. It is clear, to start with, that Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic is referring to obligations under international law. It's clear. And then he adds to it: It has to be a two-way process. The Muslims and the Croats accepted that. And he said -- Mr. Owen asked me: Why did you insist on a two-way process. And he says: "But when the Serbs from Zvornik returned to Zenica, then the Muslims from Prijedor will return to Prijedor; therefore, it must be a two-way process." When I read this as a non-native English-speaking person, first of all, I'd like to correct on the transcript when you earlier read this part it said when the Serbs from Zvornik returned to Zenica, whereas the text reads when they return to Zenica. I -- just on the basis of plain language I see the following ambiguity. You could understood it to be but only when Serbs from Zvornik return to Zenica, then the Muslims from Prijedor will return to Prijedor, then it's understood as a kind of a condition and not -- unless the Serbs return, which could implicate that if the Serbs do not return to Zenica that there would be no way of allowing the Muslims to go to Prijedor. The second way of reading it -- and please correct me if linguistically I'm wrong, and I'm also looking to Mr. Josse who is also very much a native English-speaking person. The other way I -- and I have of course to deal with the English. The other way I could understood it is that if you insist on the right of Muslims to return to Prijedor, then of course the Serbs would also have the right to return to Zenica. That's -- both would be two ways, and I see this ambiguity from a point of view of language. If you disagree with me, I'd like you, perhaps, to discuss it with Mr. Josse. So therefore, the plain language here, as I read it, does not -- at least whatever Mr. Krajisnik would say, and of course he doesn't read the English. He receives the translation in B/C/S. So I see a problem here just for you to know and for you to comment on as far as the English language is concerned, if I misunderstood it, and I'm of course to take that into account if further questions are put to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask Mr. Krajisnik one question, if I may, Your Honour, before moving on to a very closely related matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, is it the case that Dr. Karadzic is there saying that this is a -- that he's explaining to the deputies a method by which the agreement about the right of refugees and displaced persons to return can effectively be frustrated and is saying, in effect, that's a way of being -- of signing an agreement of being a bit cunning and getting what the Serbs want. Is that it or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is not saying that. In practice, Serbs did not return to Zenica, whereas Muslims did return to Prijedor. He was aware of the fact that intervention -- I understand your question. I'm going to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I interrupt again. You are again mixing up what happened later and what was said at the time of this meeting, and I invited you not to do so because it confuses very much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like to turn to the 53rd Session, please, found at tab 13.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I don't have any of these transcripts with me, and I had no opportunity to revise them before. I have only one transcript of one session. That's why I need to read the text in order to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever you need time to read the context, please ask and we'll give you an opportunity to read a few of the lines before and after that as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The portion of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the portion of Dr. Karadzic's remarks to which I want to draw your attention is found at 02154335, beginning at the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, at page 29 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just tell me which session this was and on which date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 53rd Session, held on 28 August 1995. There Dr. Karadzic begins by reciting the following -- explaining the full catalogue of human rights and fundamental freedoms and --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Is it page 35? I don't have page 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Here's an extra copy of that particular page if it's difficult to find or missing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 36, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 4335, beginning at the last paragraph of that page.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... copy. I jump from 35 to 37, and therefore from 334 to 336. Thank you. We now received it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic says: "The full catalogue of human rights," and then inserted by hand, "fundamental freedoms as listed in international instruments will be observed, including the right of refugees and displaced persons to be able to return to their homes." He's reciting the provisions contained. And continues: "We have now added which must be an overall process. They don't know what that is, so they keep shifting the first part of the sentence. That's our intention to say: All right. Everyone has the right to return to his home after the war, if that is an overall process. Now, what does that mean, an overall process? That means that the Muslims from Kozluk can return to Kozluk if the Serbs from Kozluk return to Zenica. If they don't want to return, then we need -- and if they cannot return, then we need a new war to exchange that, and that's why I think we should always insist on this. So an overall process, either overall or not at all. We can act the Serbian Cyrillic way and tell it all to their face, or we can be a bit cunning. We do have to be a bit cunning." Now, there isn't Mr. Karadzic or Dr. Karadzic explaining to the deputies the purpose and intended effect of the inclusion of the overall process provision?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he does not explain the intention. It says: "If they can't return," if they can't. If you take that into account, then -- then it's correct. Not if they don't want to return, but if they can't return, in that case the assumption would be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any translation problem? Because, Mr. Krajisnik, I read the following: "If they don't want to return, then we need -- and if they cannot return, then we need a war to exchange that." It says both, at least in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes? Okay, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If that is the motivation, if they cannot return, then the answer is yes. And indeed they were prevented from returning; you know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, that's a disingenuous interpretation of that passage. For what other reason could Dr. Karadzic have to describe it as cunning than that it has the effect of undercutting and undermining the provisions otherwise in the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will explain. The only reason why Mr. Karadzic accepted that everybody could return to their home is because during the war it was impossible for people to return. So he was trying to explain. It was cunning to explain why he signed this first part. He was aware that international conventions come first, and his decision comes second. But in practice it didn't work out. It was impossible to implement, and he knew that it would be impossible to implement. He was saying this to get people to accept the plan as a whole because everybody had some objections. Some people were saying they would be allowed to return to our parts and we would not be allowed to return to theirs. I am explaining what it was all about, and it's true that what is written here is written here. And I can tell you about what happened in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think you've answered the question, Mr. Krajisnik. Before the break, let me turn to the -- another part of the 53rd Session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think this part has to be distributed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, which session is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is again the 53rd, the same session we looked at a --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I want to turn to two portions of that, the first at page 64 of the English, and page 02154381 of the B/C/S at the very bottom, Mr. Krajisnik, and continuing on to the next page. And ask you -- and I'll turn you to two portions of this, and then I'll ask you whether or not Dr. Karadzic wasn't describing exactly how the de facto situation had been created. First at page 64: "Large operations that our army had planned and carried out, the sword, the sly dog, et cetera, a few of those operations that expanded our territory in relation to what we had done in 1992 as territorials were real operations, true operations, well-planned and carried out in circumstances where we were inferior in terms of man-power and superior in terms of men and weapons. But after that, packing Muslims into smaller areas, thus achieving their concentration, we couldn't do much more." And if you could turn also, please, to page 02154387, about two-thirds of the way down that page, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, to page 68 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where Dr. Karadzic says: "So far we have been up to the task. We were a nation. Trebinja" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just let me find this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the paragraph? I found page 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. You can go down past the first paragraph and it's about 12 lines down, again beginning: "So far we have been up to the task ..." The next two sentences have the words Drvar and Trebinje in them. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the English it's located four sentences up from the bottom on page 68. "So far we have been up to the task. We were a nation. Trebinje must equally care about Drvar and Drvar about Trebinje, otherwise we are ruined. We absolutely cannot let ourselves get any ideas about them taking our traditional territories from us. To tell the truth, there are towns that we grabbed for ourselves, and there were only 30 per cent of us. I can name as many of those as you want, but we cannot give up the towns where we made up 70 per cent. Don't let this get around, but remember how many of us there were of us in Bratunac, how many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica, how many in Vlasenica, in Zvornik, et cetera. Due to strategic importance, they had to become ours, and no one is practically questioning it anymore." Now, both of those passages, Mr. Krajisnik, are an reflection of how the de facto situation, the new reality on the ground to which we have been referring this morning was created. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think the rest of that paragraph should be read out, or at least Mr. Krajisnik should examine it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would be happy to, Your Honour, that's fine. "Between Grmec and Kozara, I think Milosevic must also know that. Foreign negotiators have also been told this. Between Grmec and Kozara, nothing can belong to anyone but us because genocide has committed there. Serbian people have been killed there and the number of Muslims grew 50 per cent because of the genocide and not because of some natural development. Genocide was also committed in the Neretva valley. There. That is all I wanted to say." First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, the genocide that is referred to here is the genocide committed in World War II. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And back to my earlier question, both of the passages that were just read out from this session are an expression of the -- of how the de facto situation, the new reality on the ground, was created. Correct? And are -- excuse me, and are a reflection of that new reality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karadzic said here that he had taken parts of the territory that didn't belong to the Serbs, and he enumerated these towns. And he said we have to preserve these areas as Serb because we were 70 per cent in Krajina. And he said in those areas where genocide had been committed and Muslims got it in the end, he meant Mount Kozara and Jasenovac, and he said we had to take care of each other. And he said about those places that weren't ours and that we had taken, Bratunac and Srebrenica and others, nobody was raising that question anymore. That was clear, but you cannot have your cake and eat it. It's clear that people from those areas that did not ethnically belong to Serbs but were Serb at the moment were protesting. They wanted to stay there, and this was Karadzic's response to them. What you have put to me is correct. I've just given you a broader explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd first like to go into private session for only a very short moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. Mr. Tieger, would you -- you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, earlier today we looked at the rally in I think it was August of 1994 in Banja Luka where, among others, Mr. Brdjanin spoke, Mr. Kupresanin spoke, and you spoke. And you commented upon Mr. Kupresanin's remarks after those had been reviewed, and at 11.59.31 of the transcript you said the following. "Yes, it refers to the Muslims, but I did not comment on Mr. Brdjanin. That was a completely wrong discussion. I was commenting only on Kupresanin's statement, and rhetorically I said these wonderful statements simply to gloss over a statement I did not agree with. I will comment on Mr. Kupresanin 's statement. Mr. Kupresanin denied the existence of the Muslims. He said they were former Serbs and everybody applauded. They applauded all kinds of nonsense, and ineptly I said if the Muslims didn't want to be Serbs we had to believe them. What I meant to say by this was that they had the right to be Muslims; that's what I still think today. And then I wanted to tell all these people who were listening that it's nice to be a Serb and that it's sad that they don't want to be Serbs. But you can't tell someone that he has to be a Serb if he wants to be a Muslim. You can see that from here. But I had to put it this way because there were so many people there and I couldn't say: Kupresanin, you're a criminal. What politician would say that? I just said nicely: Well, we should believe them when they say they're Muslims. You have no right," I think, "to force someone to be a Serb if he's not. That's what I meant to say by these words. I wasn't denying the Muslims their right to be a nation." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, that's not the only time, and that wasn't the first time, that you responded to Kupresanin's comments about Muslims as a nation, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I may have commented on this at other times. This, I know, was at a rally in Banja Luka. But please excuse me, is the interpretation correct that I said that Kupresanin was a criminal? This may have been misinterpreted. I didn't use the word "criminal." I don't think I said it -- or at least I didn't mean to say it. I said something that he had something bad -- well, it would be bad for me to say he's a criminal. He's not a criminal. He's simply radical and he says the wrong things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to page -- let's turn to the 24th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly held on 8th of January, 1993. That's -- and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to turn first to page 78 of the English and page 02149934 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the English Mr. Kupresanin's comments begin at the bottom of the page and in the B/C/S in the middle of the page. And there Mr. Kupresanin, again, turns to the question of whether Muslims are a nation, saying: "We stumbled over some ideas several times in the past. Gentlemen, is the Muslim nation a nation at all? The nation that was created in Tito's conception in 1974 receives a position like the Greeks, to say the least." And then he continues talking about that, as you can see, claiming it's a deception, talking -- saying: "It is true that the Turks were here for some time, for 500 years. We threw out the Turks, we threw out the Austrians, and we threw out the Germans, and yet Bosnia isn't Serb Muslim, of a non-existent nation. Are these not Serb stupidities again? Well, if we make this mistake now, we mistake an elementary mistake like in primary school. I propose that we deny the Muslims as a nation on the next session of the Assembly." And he describes that as not a maximalist view but a realistic view. And then, Mr. Krajisnik, you respond: "I think that Mr. Kupresanin is right, and I was wrong when I once said don't put them together with us because if you push them together with us we do not know what to do with them. I think this should be corrected a little. We should really take a stand concerning whether the Muslims are a nation. Here we had one suggestion that we say that they are a Muslim sect of Turkish orientation because it would then create a discord in the Muslim world, namely Saudi Arabia and some other Muslim countries believe that the Turks are fake Muslims, who eat and drink like the others. It is known that they are not so religious. We can take a stand at this position. It is obvious that we stumble over this question all the time. We can develop a discussion about this question. We can reach conclusions and include them in the conclusions as well. Here, Vojo, you were right and I wasn't. Let us say a religious group of Turkish orientation, that would be very important to say because they are not from any Muslim world but the Muslims of Turkish orientation which is different from the real Muslims. Does anyone have anything against that the Muslims are not a nation? How about a definition as follows?" Then there's an intervention by Mr. Corda. You speak again. Mr. Knezevic speaks, and then you say: "Shall we then now take the Muslims out of Serbism forever? All right, gentlemen, can we now make up our mind and take a position that the Muslims as a nation are the communistic creation. We do not accept this artificial nation. We believe that the Muslims are a sect, a group, or a party of Turkish provenance. Does anyone have anything else to add? No. I put these conclusions to a vote. Gentlemen, who is for? Is there anyone against? Abstaining? Gentlemen, thank you. We adopted the conclusions unanimously."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- let me just -- you read a line -- I can't find the line about the Serbism, taken forever from Serbism --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's on page 80, Your Honour, and it's the third paragraph that appears there, under "president."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you moved to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, and -- as -- since we're on that page let me read. I indicated there was an intervention from Mr. Corda and then I should -- Mr. Krajisnik spoke. That's at the bottom of page 79 and continues to the top of page 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, that's the second time you're listed as speaking after Mr. Kupresanin speaks. And that should be found on page 02149935.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where you say: "Let me just explain why it isn't good. They want us to say that we're all the same. They really want to create one nation, that we're all the same only of different religion. We must say that we are different. They are a group of Turkish orientation. Well, all right, people, if we accept that they are some kind of a group, Turkish or I don't know whose, then we simply give them aces to their hands to be an independent nation. They will be more than happy to claim that they are of Turkish origin, the same as the Siptars developed theories that they are of Iloric origin. Why, we should tell them what they really are. They are unbelievers, a nation that is not a nation. That is to say a nation that would like to be a nation but has no arguments for a nation." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, when you responded to the review of Mr. -- When you talked about your comments in response to Mr. Kupresanin's comments in 1994 by saying that you disagreed with him and you didn't deny the Muslims their right to be a nation, that was just wrong, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. This here is nonsense, what Momcilo Krajisnik was saying. It's detrimental. I have to say I never thought like this. If I could distance myself from this Momcilo Krajisnik, I would. I would have to read all of this because I probably had a reason for saying this; however, the reason does not justify speaking like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, irrespective of your -- of whatever position you take now about those comments, that was the position you took in January of 1993. And on the basis of that position, you formulated and had adopted the conclusion that we just read. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We should find this. There was somebody else's intervention, somebody else who repeated all this. I think Savo Knezevic repeated all this. There was a discussion about the Vance-Owen Plan and all this contribution of mine is immoderate, it's all wrong, and it's absolutely unfair because I never denied to the Muslims the existence of their nation. However, this speech is absolutely authentic, and I'm very sorry that this Momcilo Krajisnik said what he said. But I would really like to find the background, the reason why I said this. It must have been somebody else who started this. I know what Kupresanin said, but I spoke in a very indecent way because there's no reason why anybody should not be allowed to be a Muslim, a Croat, a Serb, whatever they please. And I have to say I remember this contribution that I made, vaguely but I remember it. I remember saying this. But if you allow me to review this session in prison, I'll find the person who brought this up in the first place, after which I formulated the conclusions. But I absolutely shouldn't have said this. It was absolutely inappropriate, and I accept your criticism and, of course, I accept that it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I take it that Mr. Krajisnik will have an opportunity -- because I do understand he's -- he'll take these minutes with him in the Detention Unit so that he can comment on it, what triggered him to use these words?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the understanding was that Mr. Krajisnik would be able to take with him any documents that had been presented to him -- I should -- and I mentioned before the further understanding was that we wouldn't copy again the sessions he already had, but if the 24th Session needs to be provided, that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krajisnik, you have an opportunity to do what you should intend --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, the record should reflect that we're doing so right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's worth remembering that the binders, as I understand it, go from 1 to 23. From 24 onwards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely, they're not in the sequential order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we included 24 after we began, but in any event now Mr. Krajisnik has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to turn back in time now to 1991, and in particular to your testimony about Dr. Karadzic's speech at the Bosnian Assembly session in -- on the 14th and 15th of October, I guess the late evening of the 14th or the early morning hours of the 15th , in which he said: "This is the road that you want Bosnia and Herzegovina to take, the same highway of hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia went through. Don't think you won't take Bosnia and Herzegovina to hell and Muslim people in possible extinction because Muslim people will not be able to defend itself if it comes to war here." Now, Mr. Stewart read that out to you during the course of your examination, and you explained Dr. Karadzic's comments as simply being a repetition of what Mr. Filipovic had said earlier, and as I understood it that was your explanation of the benign aspect of Dr. Karadzic's comments. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained to Mr. Stewart what Mr. Karadzic had stated and what the papers wrote about that, why he gave that statement that upset the public, and I provided it on that DVD to the Trial Chamber. As for this statement, if you want to know, I can comment upon it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if I understood you correctly - and please correct me if I'm wrong - you wanted the Court to understand that Dr. Karadzic's remarks should not be misinterpreted as a threat because he claimed that he was simply repeating what Dr. Filipovic had said. Is that basically it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two things to be said here. I presented a new fact about how Mr. Karadzic explained his statement before the Assembly, and I provided a document to support that. And as for the "quality" of that statement, I have to say I read through that statement ten times in its entirety. And it has never been read in its entirety before the Trial Chamber. He repeated ten times: I am not threatening, I am not threatening, I am not threatening. And we should take a look at that. I heard him speak on that occasion, and I was embarrassed but I didn't understand his tone to be threatening. You will see there are three or four entire pages dedicated to his pleas for an agreement. He said: I am not threatening. I am begging you, meaning the other two sides. However, the passage most often quoted before the public is the ugliest passage that sounds threatening. However, I know exactly what he said, all of it, and there is even video footage of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, when you say it's not a threat, but that mean that Dr. Karadzic was saying something to the effect of: Please, don't make us do this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic said: I'm not threatening. I'm not threatening. I'm not threatening. And then he said exactly what you now suggested in a different context, but he said: I'm not threatening, please. He said that several times, and that's why I understood it was not a threat, it was a warning. And if the Muslims had been scared by his words, they would not have voted for the platform and the memorandum, as they did, which means they weren't frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that you cited Mr. Filipovic's remarks to explain further to the Trial Chamber that this was not a threat? Because Dr. Filipovic had said it also?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I presented a new fact to the Trial Chamber, a fact that wasn't known. And I know it because I asked Mr. Karadzic about it, and he explained to me the same thing he explained to the press. I presented it to the Trial Chamber so that the Trial Chamber should know Mr. Karadzic's own explanation of why he said what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, perhaps it's useful to look at what Mr. Filipovic actually said, and in that respect if we could turn to tab 26, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Filipovic said; I only know what the press wrote about it. I don't remember the statement of Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just one moment, if I may have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, we've moved through that first bundle of materials and we're just retrieving the next bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, could I ask my learned friend is there an index with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If there's not one available at the moment, I'm sure one is -- can be produced or can be made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's fine. I just wanted to know whether there was one at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to be directing your attention to page 03531269 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it's page 4, Your Honours, of the English, beginning at approximately the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for ease of reference, the portion to which I am referring occurs shortly after a number of statistics, including 90 per cent, 92.1, and 55, et cetera. So you'll see a lot of numbers and then the portion below --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which session is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is the -- you mean which date of the session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean which document and which date, if you know. I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is Dr. -- this is Mr. Filipovic speaking at the session of the Bosnian Assembly at which Dr. Karadzic also made his address. That's the session from October --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the same session?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we just have the date, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have looked at several sessions in which Mr. Karadzic spoke, one of them being the 42nd Session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe this is from the first date of the session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of 14th/15th --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, of the 10th, I think, but I'll double-check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 10th of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of October, I believe. But again I can double-check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please tell us whenever you find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Filipovic states: "What does this mean? This means that the separation of the SAO Krajinas is nothing but the establishment of ethnically clean territories because the consequence of regionalisation is the transport of people. That transport already exists. Refugees from Herzegovina are already coming to Bosnia. Refugees are leaving Sipovo-Kljuc. Territory will be ethnically cleansed, but considering quantitative relations, this ethnic cleansing of the territory will not lead to the creation of an ethnically clean Bosnian Krajina or a Bosnian Krajina or Bosnia-Herzegovina or remaining Bosnia where the Muslims are out-voted. It will again be Bosnia-Herzegovina or its remainder in which the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims will co-exist and where there will be a 50 per cent Muslim population, so they won't be a majority, and hence history will repeat itself. This means that the permanent process of the dissolution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, its disintegration, and I'm interested in this above all because I'm convinced that the disintegration of Bosnia-Herzegovina, its regionalisation, it being reduced to something that will later also be regionalised and will dissolve is the beginning of the end of my people. This is why I want to say that we have to face the cause of this process." Now, this, Mr. Krajisnik, is a clear expression of Mr. Filipovic's concerns about and objections to actions being taken by the SDS in respect to the regionalisation of Bosnia and to any form of ethnic division of Bosnia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic was saying that we had to reach agreement, otherwise Bosnia and Herzegovina would break up. He was saying this on occasion of the historic agreement, and the rest of his -- of his contribution provides an explanation. He says: Unless we manage to reach an agreement, my people will disappear. He did say that, although not in the same language as Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Filipovic was expressing his fear about what would happen to Muslims at the hands of the Bosnian Serbs or the SDS, right, if agreement wasn't reached?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me read to you the sentence. "The cause is that the Serbs feel that Bosnia and Herzegovina doesn't guarantee them the rights they want. We have to open discussions and seek agreements, which is the only political logic and the only way. There are no other means except war. In today's conditions, we cannot ensure permanent order, security, and the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And he was expressing his concerns in the passage I read out, that the impact on the Bosnian Muslims of SDS policies and actions. That's what he was concerned about. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about regionalisation. Correct. He was against regionalisation, thinking that it was a division of Bosnia. He advocated instead a historic agreement whereby Bosnia would remain in Yugoslavia. That was the position of Mr. Filipovic and he was presenting it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And beyond that, the idea that Dr. Karadzic was merely quoting Mr. Filipovic and that somehow justified or explained his remarks is something that Mr. Filipovic has, himself, not only denied but explained as completely untrue. Isn't that right? Dr. Filipovic, like many, many others in attendance understood that Dr. Karadzic was making a threat against Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This preceded the contribution by Mr. Karadzic. The meaning of these words is clear. Mr. Filipovic says: Unless we agree, the resulting threat to my people would be disappearance. What Mr. Karadzic later said to the press was his justification of what he said before the Assembly. It's not I who had made that statement, it was Mr. Karadzic. But just compare these two things. Mr. Filipovic is speaking here, advocating an integral Bosnia within Yugoslavia. And he says: My people will disappear if we accept regionalisation, if we don't manage to reach an agreement. And Mr. Karadzic said basically the same thing. He said we had to agree, we had to seek an agreement. But maybe the Muslims understood it differently. If you look at the entire statement, you'll see that what I'm saying is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm suggesting to you that Mr. Filipovic understood it as a threat, Dr. Karadzic meant it as a threat, and that you understood that that was meant as a threat or a warning about the extinction or physical destruction of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, find the date of this session. This must be before the statement by Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Filipovic could not have understood something as a threat if he hadn't heard it at all. He was afraid of regionalisation, he was against it, he was advocating reaching an agreement. He was against the dissolution of Bosnia, and he was right there. He wanted a Bosnia within Yugoslavia. Look at the date, whereas what Karadzic said was said on the 14th or 15th of October. Take a look at the date of this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Rather than discussing the logic of that, let's turn to the three prongs of that issue, first to tab 27, if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the date of this Bosnian Assembly session, which you guessed would be the 10th of October, becomes more relevant in view of the answer of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said Mr. Filipovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just note -- I don't think there's any question that if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said Mr. Filipovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I don't think there's any question that it preceded the remarks of Dr. Karadzic. I mean, that's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the understanding of Mr. Filipovic that this was a threat does not find its basis in --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what he said on the 10th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, if we could turn to tab 27 --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me understand this. Is it beyond dispute that this statement was made before Karadzic's statement? That's all I want to know. Yes. All right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 27 contains an article from March 1994 by Mr. Filipovic. I want to direct your attention, Mr. Krajisnik's attention to a couple of portions. The first is found in the English at page 2 and on the first page, I believe, of the printed article where Mr. Filipovic says: "In his well-known address at a session of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Karadzic did nothing else but roughly embody and illustrate this strategy aimed at creating and sustaining a third Yugoslavia by means of a genocidal threat towards Bosnia and Herzegovina. His programme was based on the position: Either you accept Yugoslavia or you disappear as a state and as a people." So I think we can agree that there Mr. Filipovic makes clear his understanding that Dr. Karadzic's remarks were a threat directed at the Muslim people, a threat that they would be physically destroyed as a people. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1994 he made this comment. In 1991, just like Karadzic, he advocated Bosnia remaining within Yugoslavia, in July 1991. Those are facts. He did make these comments in 1994 referring to the statements made by Mr. Karadzic in 1991. A month before that he had advocated Bosnia within Yugoslavia. He and Mr. Zulfikarpasic suggested a historical agreement and people still say today that this could have saved Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to interrupt you. Here again a similar thing seems to happen, that is how Mr. Filipovic understood the language by Mr. Krajisnik [sic] as threatening or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Karadzic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karadzic, yes. As he -- well, the transcript says "Karadzic." I don't know what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not all the same, Mr. Krajisnik, and you know the Chamber doesn't take that view. The -- we are mixing up again. Even if Mr. Filipovic at the time would be in favour of Yugoslavia, that does not exclude him from telling us in 1994 that he considered this language to the threatening. You're mixing up argument and facts at this moment, and I invite you to first look at what he said -- what he writes here, whether you could agree with Mr. Tieger that he, at least in 1994, says that at the time when he heard it or on the basis of thoughts developed later on, he considered this to be threatening. And a totally different question is whether, apart from the threat, he would be in favour of staying within Yugoslavia or not, either in 1991 or 1994. We are mixing up at this moment several matters, and I would like to avoid that as much as possible, because questions and answers do not match anymore. I'm also looking at the clock, Mr. Tieger. I am aware that I'm interrupting. But before we adjourn for the day, Mr. Krajisnik, and before I instruct where do you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or are still about to give, we have the correction -- well, correction. The review of the B/C/S and English given by the CLSS. Mr. Josse, you are perfectly right. There was a need to review because where -- and I think that's the most relevant line. The remainder will be filed. But where the transcript -- the uncorrected transcript read: "I thought that when there is a map being drawn, that there should be as many Serb territories as possible, as in accordance with the -- where the Serbs did not have a majority." The review brings us, and the report includes the B/C/S, but the review brings us to the following text: "I thought that when the map was being drawn, there should be as many Serb territories as possible, according to the principle envisaged by the Lisbon agreement, not to be megalomaniacs and demand areas where the Serbs did not have a majority." So the portion did not appear in the English transcript, as you read it at first, which I would say changes the meaning of this portion of the testimony by a full 180 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We're grateful to the Chamber for organising that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it will be filed so that -- and of course the transcript will be corrected. That means that the definitive transcript will reflect the testimony as given by Mr. Krajisnik. Then we will adjourn for the day. We will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. And I remind the parties that we will have an early finish tomorrow; that would be approximately 20 minutes earlier than usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, before we recess, can we have the bundle returned so we can extract the relevant portions and then return them to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that can be done before Mr. Krajisnik leaves this building?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Usher, you are required -- no, no, not at this moment, but could you please assist Mr. Tieger in having this material returned. And then you will receive whatever has been dealt with already, Mr. Krajisnik. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 31st day of May, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
